source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / ASPIRE Project, IFAD-funded - "ដំណាំក្រូចថ្លុង" (Pomelo Cultivation Guide), 2017, 90pp
text:
Several large swallowtail butterfly species lay eggs on citrus and their caterpillars (ដង្កូវក្រូច) feed on leaves, sometimes stripping young trees of foliage. The source names three: the common lime/citrus swallowtail (Papilio demoleus), the common Mormon (ដង្កូវក្រូចខ្មៅ, Papilio polytes), and the great Mormon (ដង្កូវក្រូចធំ, Papilio memnon) - all in family Papilionidae, order Lepidoptera.

Young caterpillars are dark and are camouflaged to resemble bird droppings, a defense that makes them easy to overlook on a casual inspection; older caterpillars turn green and can be well camouflaged against citrus leaves. Given time, a single caterpillar can consume a significant number of leaves as it grows through its larval stages before pupating and emerging as a butterfly.

Because these caterpillars are large, visible once spotted, and relatively slow-moving, hand-picking and destroying caterpillars is a practical control method for smallholders, especially on young trees where leaf loss matters most; this avoids unnecessary insecticide use against a pest that a farmer walking the orchard regularly can manage directly.
